summary: The Kakatiyas, long-time vassals of the Chalukyas of Kalyani, declared independence under Rudradeva around 1163 and made Orugallu (Warangal) their capital. Ganapati (c. 1199–1262) brought almost all the Telugu-speaking lands, from the Telangana uplands to the Godavari–Krishna delta, under one rule, and his daughter Rudrama Devi governed as one of India's few reigning queens. Delhi armies made Prataparudra II a tributary in 1310, and in 1323 the future Muhammad bin Tughluq took Warangal and ended the dynasty.
details: The Kakatiyas had served the Chalukyas of Kalyani for generations from their fief at Anumakonda (Hanamkonda) in Telangana. As Chalukya power faded, Rudradeva subdued rival chiefs and, around 1163, proclaimed himself a sovereign king; from then on Kakatiya inscriptions used Telugu rather than Kannada. He built the Thousand Pillar Temple at Anumakonda and began moving the capital to nearby Orugallu, modern Warangal, which the Kakatiya dynasty article dates to 1195. Rudradeva died around 1195, perhaps killed fighting the Yadava king Jaitugi, though historians dispute this. His brother Mahadeva succeeded him.

The Kakatiyas' western neighbours, the Yadavas (Seunas) of Devagiri, were expanding fast. King Mahadeva was killed in a conflict with the Yadava kingdom, dated to 1198-1199, and his son Ganapati was captured. While Ganapati was a prisoner, the Kakatiya kingdom suffered revolts and invasions, and loyal commanders such as Rudra of the Recherla family held it together. The Yadavas eventually released Ganapati and installed him as their vassal, and he married Somaladevi, a daughter of the Yadava king Jaitugi. The kingdom survived, and its greatest reign began under Yadava overlordship.

Once free, Ganapati set out to win the rich Telugu-speaking lowlands of coastal Andhra, where the Velanati Choda chiefs had grown weak. His commanders, the Malyala chief Chaunda and his son Kata, campaigned as far as Divi island in the Krishna delta, and by 1201 Kakatiya power reached Vijayawada. Ganapati also backed the Nellore chief Tikka and, according to a 1228 inscription, plundered the Chola capital, probably Kanchi. A 1231 inscription says he annexed Velanadu and Divi. In the 1230s the kingdom reached the Godavari and Krishna deltas, uniting the Telangana uplands with the coast.

In the south, Ganapati had long protected the Telugu Choda rulers of Nellore, but a new power was rising: the Pandyas of Madurai under Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan I. While the Kakatiya army was busy fighting the Kadava chief Kopperunchinga, the main Pandya army marched on Nellore. In the Battle of Muttukuru in 1263 the Pandyas captured the city and killed its ruler, Manuma-siddhi II, Ganapati's ally, and also claimed victories over the Kakatiyas and the Seunas. The Kakatiyas lost their southern sphere of influence, a setback that clouded the end of Ganapati's long reign.

Ganapati had no son, so around 1260 he made his daughter Rudrama co-regent under the male regnal name Rudra-deva Maharaja. By 1263 she appears to have been ruling alone, though she was not formally anointed until at least 1269. She put down an early revolt, recovered some of the lands lost to the Pandyas, and turned back invasions by the Yadavas from the west and the Gajapatis of Odisha from the north-east. She also strengthened Warangal fort, raising its inner wall and adding an outer wall with a moat. The Venetian traveller Marco Polo, who visited around 1293, praised her rule.

In the 1270s and 1280s the Kayastha chief Ambadeva, a Kakatiya feudatory, built an independent kingdom in the south of the realm, with support from the Yadavas and the Pandyas. Rudrama lost much of her southern territory to him. An inscription at Chandupatla, dated 27 November 1289, records a gift for the merit of Rudrama and her general Mallikarjuna, who had both recently died, probably in battle against Ambadeva's forces. Older histories had her ruling until 1295. Her grandson Prataparudra II succeeded her and set out to win back the lost lands.

Prataparudra II reorganised the army and struck back. In 1291-92 his forces drove Ambadeva out of Tripurantakam, and in 1309 they ended Kayastha rule in Mulikinadu. He also attacked the Yadavas, who had backed Ambadeva. The 1294 Raichur Fort inscription of his feudatory Gona Vithala records the capture of the Adavani and Tumbala forts, in today's Bellary district, and of forts in the Raichur Doab, and says Vithala took Raichur and built strong fortifications there. The Kakatiya kingdom now reached west into the contested lands between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers.

Alauddin Khalji, Sultan of Delhi, had already plundered the Yadava capital Devagiri in 1296, and he saw the Kakatiya kingdom as another rich source of plunder. In 1303 he sent an army under Malik Chajju and Fakhruddin Jauna into Telangana. The Kakatiya forces resisted strongly and defeated it at the Battle of Upparapalli, and the expedition ended in disaster. The victory kept the kingdom free for a few more years. But Delhi had shown its interest in the Deccan, and its next attack on Warangal would be far larger and better prepared.

In 1309 Alauddin sent his general Malik Kafur to force Prataparudra to accept Delhi's overlordship. Kafur's army reached Orugallu (Warangal) in January 1310 and breached the outer fort after a siege of about a month. In February Prataparudra surrendered. Alauddin did not want to annex the kingdom: Prataparudra kept his throne but had to make symbolic acts of submission and pay annual tribute. Kafur returned to Delhi in June 1310 with huge wealth, probably including the Koh-i-Noor diamond, along with 20,000 horses and 100 elephants. The kingdom remained, but as a tributary of Delhi.

After Alauddin died, Prataparudra stopped paying tribute, saying the road to Delhi was too dangerous. In 1318 the new sultan, Mubarak Shah, sent his general Khusrau Khan to Orugallu with siege machines never before seen in the region. Prataparudra had to submit again. This time Delhi arranged a very public humiliation: the king bowed towards Delhi from the ramparts of his own capital. His annual tribute was reset at 100 elephants and 12,000 horses, and he had to give up five districts. The kingdom still kept its own king, but its independence was now a fiction.

In 1320 a revolution in Delhi replaced the Khaljis with Ghiyasuddin Tughluq, and Prataparudra asserted his independence again. In 1321 the new sultan sent his son, Jauna Khan, to besiege Orugallu. The siege dragged on for about six months. Rumours of the sultan's death split Jauna Khan's army, many officers left, and the attackers withdrew to Devagiri to regroup. Prataparudra celebrated by opening his grain stores for public feasting. The victory seemed to restore the kingdom, but it left Warangal short of supplies when the enemy came back.

Jauna Khan, the future Sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq, returned in 1323 with a reinforced army. After a five-month siege, with few supplies left, Prataparudra was forced to submit, and the Kakatiya dynasty article dates the end of the dynasty to 9 November 1323. Orugallu was renamed Sultanpur and the kingdom became a province of the Delhi Sultanate. Prataparudra died while being taken to Delhi as a prisoner, perhaps by suicide on the banks of the Narmada. Telugu chiefs such as Kapaya Nayaka later held Warangal, but the Kakatiya line was over.
